title: Stack-scan and cacheline effects on request hotpath (sampling notes)
content:
Purpose:
Quick working notes from a set of sampling and perf-counter experiments focused on an intermittent ~6-18ms tail in small-request (<= 512 B) end-to-end latency. Hypothesis space expanded from tokenizer/parse CPU to memory-system effects (LLC misses / cacheline churn) and Python stack-scan/GC interactions when worker threads are hot-swapped.

Summary / tl;dr:
- Repro: small synthetic requests routed through api-gateway -> request-preproc (pyshim) -> tokenization (Rust FFI) -> serving runtime request queue -> GPU candidate path. Intermittent spikes correlate with user request bursts and thread handoffs.
- Sampling + perf counters show two recurring signals: (1) increased LLC-load-misses on the worker handling preproc / small JSON parse, (2) anomalous pause windows where user-space stacks show long time spent in 'madvise/stack scanning' and in Python GC safepoint checks.
- Changing allocator (jemalloc->tcmalloc) and reducing GC thresholds reduced incidence by ~40% in our stress bench. Increasing worker pool size reduced queueing but shifted spikes to other workers.

Environment / baseline:
- branch: main @ 6b9f3d (serving-runtime)
- image: rw-inference-serving:prod-2026-02
- testbed: c6gn.8xlarge(ARM) and c6i.8xlarge(x86) for cross-arch comparison
- Python runtime: 3.11.4 (pyshim embedding single interpreter per worker)
- Tokenizer: rust-tokenize v0.4.1 via pyo3 FFI
- Bench harness: synthetic small-request fanout 1000 qps for 60s, 1.5x burst pulses every 5s

How I looked: quick checklist of tools used
- perf record --call-graph dwarf -F 250 -a -g -p <pid> (sampling during burst)
- perf stat -e L1-dcache-loads,L1-dcache-load-misses,LLC-loads,LLC-load-misses,cycles,instructions -p <pid>
- flamegraph from perf script + stackcollapse-perf.pl
- py-spy --native --subprocesses attached for Python stacks (low overhead)
- heap-profiler snapshots for jemalloc
- strace -c for syscall patterning

Notable observations:
1) LLC load misses spike during the first 10-30s of a burst window on worker threads that had been idle ~>10s. On c6i results: LLC-load-misses per second rose 6x compared to steady-state.
2) Flamegraphs show a tight column of time attributed to 'PyInterpreterState->eval_frame' then C-level safepoint/stackscan calls (function names obfuscated by C extensions). py-spy stacks show 'gc.collect' and 'ceval.c: PyEval_EvalFrameEx' stacks interleaved.
3) Strace shows increased madvise/mprotect syscalls immediately prior to the latency spike window on those threads (page advisory calls consistent with lazy stack growth or thread-stack touching).
4) Repro across archs: ARM shows less pronounced LLC effect but more frequent safepoint jitter. x86 shows strong LLC signal.

Hypotheses (ordered by likelihood):
- H1: Cold worker thread stacks cause page faults/stack growth at first request after idle, producing syscall/madvise and causing cacheline churn as kernel touches pages => latency spike.
- H2: Python GC safepoint checks are colliding with request-critical code paths due to allocation patterns in preproc (short-lived objects + many small lists/dicts) causing STW-ish pauses for thread scanning.
- H3: Allocator fragmentation with jemalloc leads to cache-unfriendly allocations (larger spans crossing cachelines) causing increased LLC misses on hot path.
- H4: Tokenizer FFI boundary causes copies with poor alignment, inducing extra cache misses when marshaling small payloads.

Quick experiments run (and results):
- Disable jemalloc (LD_PRELOAD removed) -> tcmalloc fallback: tail spike incidence down 38% (n=10 runs). Perf counters show ~25% drop in LLC-load-misses.
- Bump Python GC thresholds (PYTHONMALLOC / set_threshold) by 2x: reduced explicit gc.collect occurrences in traces and reduced spike count by 15%.
- Touch stacks eagerly on worker start (pthread_attr_setstacksize + manual mlock test) — prototype: pre-touching 256KB of stack on thread init removed the madvise/mprotect calls and reduced the cold-worker spike occurrences substantially in local runs.
- Change FFI marshal to use preallocated pinned buffer path (avoid temp Vec allocations) — preliminary microbench shows small improvement (~6% CPU) but not large impact on LLC misses.

Open data snippets (from perf stat, averaged over 3 bursts):
- Baseline (jemalloc): LLC-load-misses: 4.8M/s, cycles: 1.2G/s
- tcmalloc run: LLC-load-misses: 3.6M/s, cycles: 1.1G/s

Immediate actionable mitigations (low risk):
- Pre-touch worker stacks on spawn (worker framework change) — cheap and removes stack-growth syscall cost.
- Increase GC thresholds for the preproc worker group (configurable pool) to reduce safepoint frequency for small-request path.
- Add allocator toggle in runtime image (ship with tcmalloc build for a week canary) and monitor LLC counters in production metric set.

Longer-term probes / TODOs:
- Investigate jemalloc tuning (decay time, background thread) vs tcmalloc for real workload. Add microbench harness to emulate small allocation churn of preproc pipeline.
- Add lightweight BPF trace to correlate madvise/mprotect events to specific worker IDs and correlate with perf counters.
- Evaluate per-worker arena pinning to reduce cross-thread cacheline bounce when multiple workers touch shared metadata. This is invasive but could reduce LLC churn.
- Deeper tokenization marshal audit: ensure buffers are 64-byte aligned and explore zero-copy wire-format for small payloads.
- Revisit pyshim design: experiment with subinterpreters (PEP 554 style) to isolate GC safepoints (tradeoffs noted: subinterpreters add complexity for extension modules).

Notes / random findings:
- Increasing worker count reduced mean latency but did not remove spikes; spikes redistributed. This supports a memory-system origin rather than queueing alone.
- On x86, using hugepages for runtime heap in test removed ~10% of LLC misses but introduced other noise; needs more study.

Next steps (concrete):
1) Patch worker start to pre-touch 256KB stack + ship to canary cluster (Marcus to own patch). Linked PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/912
2) Create A/B canary with jemalloc vs tcmalloc, add perf counter dashboards (LLC-load-misses per-request) and run 7-day experiment (Asha owns measurement plan). RW ticket RW-2738.
3) Add BPF trace for madvise/mprotect and map to worker id — small PoC (Sophie) to capture correlation data.

Questions / discussion items:
- Are we comfortable shipping tcmalloc as image default to reduce immediate tail? Risk: different fragmentation behavior under sustained large-batch workloads.
- If pre-touch stack removes spikes in production, should we still pursue allocator change? both could be complementary.

Appendix: quick perf command examples used during capture
- perf stat -e LLC-load-misses,cycles,context-switches -p $PID -- sleep 30
- perf record -F 250 -g -p $PID -- sleep 20; perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf-flame.svg

Unresolved:
- exact root cause of Python-layer safepoint calls remain fuzzy; need BPF to tie kernel syscall windows to Python frame events.

End of notes — this is a working doc, rough artifacts above. Will iterate after PoC runs and canary results.
